newsitem.title: ZAIRE: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO - Kabila's Congo verges on bankruptcy, looks to mines.
newsitem.headline: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO - Kabila's Congo verges on bankruptcy, looks to mines.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo is teetering on the brink of bankruptcy and is looking to its mines to help save it, Kabila's mining minister said on Monday.

Matutulo Kambale told state television in an interview that mining deals struck with what used to be Zaire would have to be renegotiated with the new government, formed after Kabila's rebels toppled veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko on May 17.

But he added that the Kabila administration, keen to create jobs and rebuild the country's shattered infrastructure, was happy to offer mining concessions in return for payment in kind -- such as road construction.

In the capital Kinshasa's open-air "Wall Street" currency black market the U.S. dollar firmed on Monday with money changers aligning their rate more closely to that recommended by Kabila's new administration.

"We are practically bankrupt...the situation in which we find ourselves is quite catastrophic," Matutulo said. "We will not go begging from the outside," he added, echoing a common theme of self-reliance among Kabila ministers.
Some ministers, among them transport minister Henri Mova Sankanyi, preach state intervention to protect public services.
Mova, who favours a state airline and railways, and other ministers have complained of foreign companies creaming off profits which they say should remain in the country.

Matutulo said there was a role for foreign investors provided the terms were right. "Our mining policy is simple. We bring in people asking them to respect the cardinal principles - - no monopoly," he said.

"Our policy is to bring in the maximum number of visitors so that we can give jobs to (our) people. It serves no purpose keeping the minerals in the ground at a time when they could benefit everyone."
On mining contracts signed under Mobutu, the minister said:

"If there were agreements with the previous government, we will accept them but on condition they are ratified, they must therefore be renegotiated because we do not know exactly under what conditions all these accords were signed."

Reserves of copper, cobalt, gold, diamonds and other minerals make Africa's third largest nation, potentially one of its richest. Under Mobutu, its national wealth was stolen or squandered in a morass of corruption and administrative chaos.
Kabila's Congo still uses the battered new zaire currency which hundreds of traders, mostly middle-aged women, hawk in large wads in markets and at cross-roads across the city.

On Monday, one U.S. dollar fetched 115,000 new zaires -- against an "official" exchange rate of 125,000 to the dollar. On Friday, when Kabila's administration set the latest rate at 125,000 new zaires, the dollar fetched 90,000 to 100,000.
Kabila's administration says it will fix the rate every Friday, after consulting bankers and the business community.
The aim, officials say, is to break with the past and impose a measure of discipline after the monetary mayhem of Mobutu's corrupt and administratively chaotic Zaire.
On May 16, the eve of the fall of Kinshasa to Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo, a dollar bought 180,000 new zaires.
The new zaire firmed on May 19, after the rebels entered the city, jumping 60 percent to 70,000 to a dollar.

"We will rejoin the official rate slowly but surely," money dealer Otis Yeye said, adding that to have switched to the official rate earlier would have meant large losses on dollars they had already brought.

Maurice Enbgondu, another dealer, said Mobutu's people forced up the dollar by flooding the market with new zaires. "The authorities will only regulate the market to avoid the lurches we knew in the past. The money changers will follow them," he added, noting Kabila had the benefit of the doubt.
